summary: Proposes an SDP attribute to state the RTCP port in a session. SDP assumes the ports used are consecutive, but a NAT that maps ports can break the ordering. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Session descriptions list the port for the media itself, and expect the control port to be the next one up. A NAT that renumbers ports breaks that rule. This RFC adds a line to the session description that names the control port explicitly.

questions: what is the sdp rtcp attribute
why does rtcp need its own port in sdp
how does nat break rtcp ports
subtitle: Lets a session description name the RTCP port exactly, so media still works when a NAT renumbers ports.

tldr.problem: A media session needs two UDP ports, one for RTP and one for RTCP, and SDP assumes they are consecutive. A NAT that maps ports does not preserve that order, so the RTCP port on the public side is unknown.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an SDP attribute, a=rtcp:, that states the RTCP port and optionally the RTCP address. It may appear at media level only, and peers that do not understand it can ignore it.
tldr.outcome: A session behind a port-mapping NAT can still set up its control channel, provided the host has learned its translated ports, for example with STUN. The RFC says the attribute should not be used for other applications.

facts.label: Attribute form
facts.value: a=rtcp: followed by the port and an optional address

facts.label: Port normally assumed
facts.value: The next higher (odd) port after the RTP port

today: RFC 3605 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With Mapped Ports
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes the parameters of media streams used in multimedia sessions. When a session requires multiple ports, SDP assumes those ports have consecutive numbers.

When a session crosses a network address translation device that also uses port mapping, the ordering of ports can be destroyed by the translation. The session invitation protocol (SIP) is often used to establish such sessions, and one or both ends are often hidden behind such a device. The SDP text must then document the IP addresses and UDP ports as they appear on the public Internet side of the NAT.

Audio and video are typically sent using RTP, which requires two UDP ports, one for the media and one for the control protocol (RTCP). SDP carries only one port number per media and states that other ports used by the media application, such as the RTCP port, should be derived algorithmically from the base media port. RTCP port numbers were necessarily derived that way in older versions of RTP such as RFC 1889, but that restriction has now been lifted, so there is a need to specify RTCP ports explicitly in SDP. Implementations adhering to the earlier RFC 1889 specification may not be able to make use of the attributes in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP uses two ports: one for the sound or video, one for the reports that go back about quality. SDP only writes down the first one and expects the second to be the next number. A NAT that swaps port numbers breaks that expectation.

sections.title: The RTCP Attribute
sections.content:
The main part of the solution is the declaration of an SDP attribute for documenting the port used by RTCP. The attribute is used when that port is not the next higher, odd, port number following the RTP port described in the media line. It is a value attribute and follows the general syntax of RFC 2327, a=<attribute>:<value>. The name is the ASCII string rtcp in lower case, and the value is the RTCP port number and optional address.

The formal description of the attribute uses this ABNF:

rtcp-attribute =  "a=rtcp:" port  [nettype space addrtype space
                         connection-address] CRLF

The port, nettype, addrtype and connection-address tokens are defined as specified in the SDP Grammar appendix of RFC 2327. Example encodings are:

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
a=rtcp:53020

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
a=rtcp:53020 IN IP4 126.16.64.4

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
a=rtcp:53020 IN IP6 2001:2345:6789:ABCD:EF01:2345:6789:ABCD

The RTCP attribute MAY be used as a media level attribute; it MUST NOT be used as a session level attribute. Though the examples relate to a method that returns only unicast addresses, both unicast and multicast values are valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute is one line added to a media description. It names the control port and may also name the address to reach it on. It belongs to one media description, not to the whole session.

sections.title: How a Host Finds Its Translated Ports
sections.content:
The solution is only useful if the host can discover the translated port numbers, meaning the value of the ports as they appear on the external side of the NAT. One possibility is to ask the cooperation of a well connected third party that will act as a server according to STUN. That gives a four step process.

  1. The host allocates two UDP port numbers for an RTP/RTCP pair.
  2. The host sends a UDP message from each port to the STUN server.
  3. The STUN server reads the source address and port of the packet, and copies them in the text of a reply.
  4. The host parses the reply according to the STUN protocol and learns the external address and port corresponding to each of the two UDP ports.

The algorithm supposes that the NAT will use the same translation for packets sent to the third party and to the SDP peer with which the host wants to establish a connection. There is no guarantee that all NAT boxes deployed on the Internet have this characteristic, and implementers are referred to the STUN specification for an extensive discussion of the various types of NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sends a packet from each of its two ports to a STUN server. The server writes back the address and port it saw. That tells the host what the outside world will use for each port.

sections.title: Two Design Questions
sections.content:
The first question is whether more than one ancillary port per media type is needed. Most media streams are transmitted using a single pair of RTP and RTCP ports. It is possible, however, to transmit a single media over several RTP flows, for example using hierarchical encoding, and SDP then encodes the port number used by RTP on the first flow and the number of flows, as in m=video 49170/2 RTP/AVP 31. In that example the media is sent over two consecutive pairs of ports: RTP for the first flow on even number 49170, RTCP for the first flow on odd number 49171, RTP for the second flow on even number 49172, and RTCP for the second flow on odd number 49173. In theory SDP could be modified to document the many ports of the separate encoding layers, but layered encoding is not much used in practice, and when used it is mostly used with multicast transmission. The translation issues in this document apply uniquely to unicast transmission, so there is no short term need for multiple port descriptions. It is more convenient and more robust to focus on the simple case in which a media is sent over exactly one RTP/RTCP stream.

The second question is why the media definition should not be changed instead of adding a new attribute. The RTP ports are documented in the media description line, so it would seem convenient to document the RTCP port in the same place. The authors considered this and rejected it for two reasons: adding an extra port number and an optional address in the media description would be awkward, and more importantly it would create problems with existing applications, which would have to reject the entire media description if they did not understand the extension. An attribute has a well defined failure mode instead: implementations that do not understand the a=rtcp attribute will simply ignore it. They will fail to send RTCP packets to the specified address, but they will at least be able to receive the media in the RTP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Most sessions use one pair of ports, so the RFC keeps things simple. Adding a new line is also safer than changing the media line, because old software that meets an unknown line just skips it and still receives the media.

sections.title: UNSAF Considerations
sections.content:
The RTCP attribute in SDP is used to enable establishment of RTP/RTCP flows through NAT. It can be used together with an address discovery mechanism such as STUN. STUN is a short term fix to the NAT traversal problem, which requires consideration of the general issues linked to unilateral self-address fixing.

The RTCP attribute addresses a very specific problem: the documentation of port numbers as they appear after address translation by a port-mapping NAT. It SHOULD NOT be used for other applications.

The authors expect that, with time, one of two exit strategies can be developed. The IETF may develop an explicit middlebox control protocol that would enable applications to obtain a pair of port numbers appropriate for RTP and RTCP. Another possibility is the deployment of IPv6, which would enable end-to-end addressing and guarantee that the two hosts can use appropriate ports. In both cases there will be no need for documenting a non-standard RTCP port with the RTCP attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Learning your own public port from outside is a short-lived trick, because it depends on the NAT behaving in a particular way. The attribute is meant only for that case, and a middlebox control protocol or IPv6 would remove the need for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This SDP extension is not believed to introduce any significant security risk to multimedia applications. One could conceive that a malevolent third party would use the extension to redirect the RTCP fraction of an RTP exchange, but this requires intercepting and rewriting the signaling packet that carries the SDP text. If an interceptor can do that, many more attacks are available, including a wholesale change of the addresses and port numbers at which the media will be sent.

To avoid attacks of this sort, when SDP is used in a signaling packet of the form application/sdp, end-to-end integrity using S/MIME is the technical method to be implemented and applied. This is compatible with SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who could change the SDP could redirect the control traffic, but such an attacker could already redirect the media itself. Signing the signaling message with S/MIME is the way to prevent that.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document defines a new SDP parameter, the attribute field rtcp, which RFC 2327 registers with IANA. The attribute field is designed for use at media level only.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute name is registered with IANA so that only this meaning is attached to it.
